chg.description: Two men who lived in western Georgia about 13,300 and 9,700 years ago form a hunter-gatherer lineage distinct from every other early genome they were compared with. Ancestry related to theirs later contributed substantially to the Yamnaya-associated herders of the steppe.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Caucasus hunter-gatherers, or CHG, are a genetic grouping that rests on very few genomes. The two that defined it come from Satsurblia and Kotias Klde, and although the men lived more than 3,000 years apart, they are more closely related to each other than to any other genome older than the Bronze Age in the study. That points to one population persisting in the region from the Late Upper Palaeolithic, the last stretch of the Old Stone Age, into the Mesolithic that followed. Their DNA also contains many long stretches in which the copies inherited from mother and father are identical, which suggests that the population was small.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The genomes place CHG on a branch that separated early from the hunter-gatherers of western Europe. One demographic model, which estimates when populations parted from the pattern of differences between their genomes, puts that split at about 45,000 years ago, or 40,000–50,000 depending on the genomes used. The same model separates CHG from the ancestors of early farmers only about 25,000 years ago, so CHG and early farmers share a branch that western hunter-gatherers do not.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Ancestry related to CHG turns up well beyond the two sites where they were sampled. North of the Caucasus, Copper Age (Eneolithic) people form a gradient running from the Caucasus to the Lower Volga that is rich in CHG-related ancestry. A 2016 study of Ice Age Europe finds CHG related to a population that contributed new ancestry to hunter-gatherers in Europe, but rules them out as that population itself: CHG carry a large share of Basal Eurasian ancestry, a deep branch of non-African ancestry that has never been sampled directly, and those Europeans do not. Among people living today, those of the southern Caucasus are the closest to CHG, which suggests some 13,000 years of continuity in the region.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The CHG-related population that contributed to the Copper Age people of the Lower Volga has not been sampled, so how their ancestry formed is still unresolved. Studies also differ on which sampled group best stands for the CHG-related part of the steppe herders' ancestry. A 2016 study uses a population related to Chalcolithic people of western Iran, who are themselves modelled as partly of CHG ancestry, while a 2024 study models steppe ancestry as about one-third CHG-related and two-thirds related to hunter-gatherers of the Middle Don, a source the authors present as previously unknown.

caveats: The map shows three individuals from two sites, so its footprint marks where CHG were sampled, not how far they ranged.
Upper Palaeolithic individuals from Dzudzuana and Kotias Klde, older than this group, are not assigned to it.

iberomaurusian-taforalt.description: Seven people associated with the Iberomaurusian culture who lived about 15,000 years ago at Taforalt in Morocco. The study that sequenced them reports that their ancestry links Near Eastern and sub-Saharan African populations.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Their DNA points in two directions. On one side, the study finds an affinity with early populations of the Near East, best represented by Natufian-associated hunter-gatherers of the Levant. On the other, about one-third of their ancestry is related to sub-Saharan Africans, and that part is best approximated as a mixture of components found today in West Africans and in East Africans. The study finds no sign that Europeans of the Palaeolithic, the Old Stone Age, contributed to their ancestry.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: A single site cannot show how widely this mixture of ancestry extended across North Africa at the time. The sub-Saharan part is matched only against present-day groups, so these results do not identify the ancient population that contributed it. And the study's summary reports an affinity with Natufians, not how or when that shared ancestry arose.

caveats: Everything on this page is checked against the study's abstract only, not its full text, so the models behind the figures have not been examined.

natufians.description: Hunter-gatherers associated with the Natufian culture of the southern Levant; the region's first farmers descended largely from hunter-gatherers related to them. Their genomes are also modelled as carrying a large share of ancestry from a deep lineage that no one has sampled directly.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The genomes come from a single site, Raqefet Cave, and date to 12,000–9,800 BCE. Their Y chromosomes, which pass from father to son and so trace a single paternal line, belong to haplogroup E, a lineage of likely African origin that the Levant's early farmers also carried. Yet across the genome as a whole, which records all of a person's ancestors, the study finds no particular affinity between Natufians and sub-Saharan Africans: one paternal line can point somewhere the rest of the ancestry does not.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Natufians, together with the earliest people sampled in Iran, carry the highest shares of Basal Eurasian ancestry in the 2016 study that defined this group. Basal Eurasian is a branch of non-African ancestry that split off before the others diversified; no genome belonging to it has been found, so its share in later people is inferred by modelling, and by extrapolation it carried little or no Neandertal DNA. The 2016 study puts the Natufian share at about 44%, a little under half. A 2019 study that uses an ancient Ethiopian genome, Mota, as its African reference finds a lower 38.5%, closer to two-fifths, so the figure shifts with the reference chosen.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Natufian-related ancestry runs on into the farming communities that followed. In one model, the Pre-Pottery Neolithic farmers of 'Ain Ghazal and Motza, 8300–6700 BCE, trace about two-thirds of their ancestry to people related to Natufians, and the Levant's early farmers share more genetic variants with Natufians than with early farmers from Iran. Far to the west, individuals associated with the Iberomaurusian culture at Taforalt in Morocco, about 15,000 years old, show an affinity with Natufians, a finding checked here against the study's abstract only.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Where the Basal Eurasian lineage lived, and how it came to be so common in the early Near East, is unknown. Because the earliest Iranian samples carry shares similar to the Natufians', Natufians cannot be shown to be the group that brought it into the region. The 2016 study offers two possible explanations: the lineage mixed thoroughly into Near Eastern populations after the main episode of interbreeding with Neandertals, or the ancestors of these populations lived in the Near East all along, in a line that took no part in that interbreeding. Even the estimate that the lineage carried little Neandertal DNA is an extrapolation with a wide margin of error.

caveats: The map shows four individuals, all from one site.

anatolia-epipaleolithic.description: One hunter-gatherer from Pınarbaşı in central Anatolia, who lived about 15,000 years ago, and the first Epipalaeolithic genome sequenced from Anatolia. Most of the ancestry of central Anatolia's early farmers traces to a population related to this individual.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This grouping is a single person from the Epipalaeolithic, the final phase of the Old Stone Age, so everything rests on one genome. Direct dating measures the remains themselves rather than the layer they lay in, and here it gives 13,642–13,073 cal BCE; "cal" marks a date corrected to calendar years. To see where the genome sits among other ancient ones, the study used principal component analysis, a method that plots genomes by their overall genetic similarity. On that plot the Pınarbaşı genome lies between western hunter-gatherers and Levantines from the Epipalaeolithic and Neolithic, and it is distinct from both.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: In one estimate, about a quarter of the Pınarbaşı individual's ancestry (24.8 percent, give or take 5.5) comes from Basal Eurasian, a lineage of non-African ancestry that split away before the other non-African lineages diversified and that no one has sampled directly. That estimate takes the ancient Ethiopian Mota genome as its African reference point. The same method puts Natufians at 38.5 percent, below the 44 percent from an earlier study, so figures of this kind move with the method and the reference chosen.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The study puts the continuity between the Pınarbaşı hunter-gatherer and the early farmers of central Anatolia at about 80–90 percent. The detail comes from models of the farmers at Boncuklu, aceramic (pre-pottery) farmers who lived about 8300–7800 BCE: 89.7 percent (plus or minus 3.9) of their ancestry derives from a population related to the Pınarbaşı individual, and the rest is Iranian- and Caucasus-related. Ceramic-period farmers who followed still derive 78.7 percent (plus or minus 3.5) of their ancestry from those earlier farmers, and add ancestry related to the Neolithic of the Levant.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: One genome cannot separate what was typical of a group from what was particular to one person, nor show how widely such hunter-gatherers lived, and the continuity result is reported for central Anatolia only. A lower-confidence result points beyond Anatolia: Iron Gates Mesolithic hunter-gatherers from the Balkans show their highest genetic affinity to the Pınarbaşı individual and their second highest to Natufians, which the authors read as a genetic link between southern Europe and the Near East older than 15,000 years, with Near Eastern gene flow into the ancestors of the Iron Gates group. That reading interprets a pattern of genetic affinity; it does not observe a movement of people.

caveats: The map shows one individual from one site, so its footprint marks where that person was found, not where hunter-gatherers of the time lived.

zagros-early-farmers.description: The first farmers of the Zagros mountains in western Iran descended largely from local hunter-gatherers, and were strongly different from the first farmers of the Levant. That contrast is part of the evidence that several differentiated hunter-gatherer populations in southwest Asia adopted farming.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This grouping gathers Early Neolithic individuals from sites in the Zagros, the mountain range of western Iran. That they farmed is supported partly by chemistry: isotopes, which are chemical signatures in remains that reflect what a person ate, indicate that the individual from Wezmeh Cave ate a diet rich in cultivated cereals.

overview.heading: When and where
overview.text: The studies behind this page name individuals from Wezmeh Cave, Tepe Abdul Hosein and Ganj Dareh. The Wezmeh Cave individual dates to 7,455–7,082 cal BCE (the "cal" marks a date corrected to calendar years) and the Ganj Dareh farmers to 8,200–7,600 BCE. Three individuals from Tepe Abdul Hosein are roughly 10,000 years old. The Wezmeh Cave and Tepe Abdul Hosein genomes differ greatly in quality: coverage, the average number of times each position was read, is about 10 for the Wezmeh Cave genome but only 0.6–1.2 for the Tepe Abdul Hosein genomes, which therefore hold far less information per person.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Ganj Dareh farmers share genetic variants at the same rate with the early farmers of Anatolia and of the Levant, which the authors read as long-term isolation of western Iran. A model puts the separation of their ancestors from those of the Anatolian farmers at about 46,000–77,000 years ago, an interval more than 30,000 years wide. Their genomes also contain fewer short stretches in which the copies inherited from mother and father are identical than any other ancient genomes the study tested, which points to a large ancestral population. In one model about 48 percent of the ancestry of Iranian Neolithic samples is Basal Eurasian, a lineage that split away before the other non-African lineages diversified and that no one has sampled directly.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: They were not ancestors of the first European farmers, nor significant contributors to present-day Europeans. Zagros Neolithic ancestry reappears in a later population: Chalcolithic (Copper Age) individuals from western Iran are modelled as a mix of Zagros Neolithic, Levant and Caucasus hunter-gatherer ancestry. A population related to them is in turn modelled as contributing between a third and 44 percent of the ancestry of Early Bronze Age steppe populations, Levantine Bronze Age populations and Chalcolithic northwestern Anatolians. Because that ancestry has several sources, these later contributions cannot be credited to the Zagros farmers alone. By the Bronze Age, Levant-, Zagros- and Anatolia-related farmer ancestries had mixed, which reduced the genetic differences across the Near East.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Whether ancestry related to early Iranian farmers spread east into South Asia is disputed. A 2016 study proposes that people related to both early Iranian farmers and steppe herders spread east into South Asia. A 2019 study of an individual from the Indus Valley Civilization finds that the Iranian-related ancestry in that person derives from a lineage that split before the ancestors of early Iranian farmers, herders and hunter-gatherers separated, which contradicts a large-scale eastward spread of western Iranian farmers. A second 2019 study describes the main ancestry of South Asians as a gradient between people related to early Iranian hunter-gatherers and people related to South and Southeast Asian hunter-gatherers.

levant-ppn-farmers.description: Pre-Pottery Neolithic farmers of the southern Levant, who descended largely from local Natufian-related hunter-gatherers but also carried Anatolian-farmer-related ancestry. Ancestry related to theirs is also modelled in a pastoralist who lived in Tanzania about 3,100 years ago.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This grouping gathers farmers of the Pre-Pottery Neolithic, the early stage of farming before pottery was in use, from sites in the southern Levant, the eastern Mediterranean region that includes present-day Israel and Jordan. Later studies use them as a reference, describing other populations by how much of their ancestry is related to Neolithic Levantines like these.

overview.heading: When and where
overview.text: A 2016 study sampled farmers from 'Ain Ghazal and Motza who lived between 8,300 and 6,700 BCE. A 2019 study added two more Pre-Pottery Neolithic B farmers, one from Kfar HaHoresh (about 7700–7600 BCE) and one from Ba'ja (7027–6685 cal BCE; "cal" marks a date corrected to calendar years). Only four sites carry the picture, so a handful of places stand for the whole region across some 1,600 years.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The Levant's early farmers share significantly more genetic variants with Natufians than with early farmers from Iran, which links their ancestry more closely to Natufian-related hunter-gatherers. In a model of the farmers from 'Ain Ghazal and Motza, about two-thirds of the ancestry is related to Natufian hunter-gatherers and about one-third to Anatolian farmers. That Natufian-related majority sets them apart from the first farmers of the Zagros, who descended largely from other local hunter-gatherers and were strongly differentiated from them.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Late Chalcolithic (Copper Age) individuals from Peqi'in Cave, dated 4500–3900 BCE, are modelled as about 57 percent Levant Neolithic-related, with the rest Iranian- and Anatolian-related. By the Bronze Age, Levant-, Zagros- and Anatolia-related farmer ancestries had mixed, which reduced the genetic differences across the Near East. In Tanzania, a pastoralist from Luxmanda who lived about 3,100 years ago is modelled with 38 percent (plus or minus 1) ancestry related to Levantine pre-pottery farmers, with Iran- or Anatolia-related sources excluded. A 2016 study likewise finds that East African ancestry related to the Near East fits Levantine early farmers better than Anatolian or early European farmers.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Whether the Levant-related ancestry in East Africa arrived by migration from the Levant or comes from a shared earlier ancestral population is open; the authors of the Tanzania study note both possibilities. The 2016 study's own reading, a lower-confidence one, is that this ancestry did not spread from the group that carried Near Eastern ancestry into Europe. The Tanzania figure also rests on a single individual.

caveats: The map's sampled range reaches 4500 BCE only because one individual from Motza has a very wide date range in the source data.

anatolia-neolithic-farmers.description: Neolithic farmers of Anatolia, whose ancestry in the central region comes largely from the local hunter-gatherers who lived there before them. Ancestry related to theirs spread west into Europe, where it makes up most of the ancestry of early farmers in the Balkans and Britain.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Two regions of Anatolia, the peninsula that makes up most of present-day Turkey, supply the evidence: central Anatolia, whose early farmers show continuity with local hunter-gatherers, and northwestern Anatolia, whose Neolithic farmers are the reference for the first farmers of Europe. The earliest farmers in the 2019 study are the aceramic farmers of Boncuklu, meaning farmers without pottery, who lived about 8300–7800 BCE; ceramic-period farmers followed them.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: In central Anatolia the early farmers' ancestry is largely local: the study of the region puts their continuity with a 15,000-year-old hunter-gatherer from Pınarbaşı at about 80–90 percent. In the models, aceramic farmers at Boncuklu derive 89.7 percent (plus or minus 3.9) of their ancestry from a population related to that hunter-gatherer, and the rest from Iranian- and Caucasus-related sources. Later ceramic-period farmers still derive 78.7 percent (plus or minus 3.5) of theirs from those earlier farmers, adding Levant Neolithic-related ancestry. A separate model places the split of the Anatolian and European farmer lineage from European hunter-gatherers at about 33,000–39,000 years ago, and from the Zagros farmers' lineage at about 46,000–77,000 years ago.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Early farmers of mainland Europe descend from a population related to Neolithic northwestern Anatolians, whom they resemble more than they resemble Levantine Neolithic farmers, by a margin of 15 standard errors. Farming reached southeastern Europe in the mid-7th millennium BCE with migrants of Anatolian-related ancestry, and about 98 percent of Balkan Neolithic ancestry is Anatolian-related in one model, the rest coming from western hunter-gatherers. In Britain the share is lower, about 74 percent on average in one model, with small hunter-gatherer contributions and no later resurgence. Across Europe, hunter-gatherer ancestry in early farmers varied by region and generally increased over time through local mixing.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The 2016 study that found the link to Europe notes that the spatial distribution of Anatolian-like farmer populations is unknown, so it does not rule out other sources for the European farmers. The continuity results concern central Anatolia, and how far they hold for northwestern Anatolia is not shown.

caveats: The map's 189 individuals come from 12 sites and span 9800–3533 BCE, more than the studies cited in the text describe.

support.text: Neolithic farmers of Anatolia, whose ancestry in the central region comes largely from the local hunter-gatherers who lived there before them.
Ancestry related to theirs spread west into Europe, where it makes up most of the ancestry of early farmers in the Balkans and Britain.

Two regions of Anatolia, the peninsula that makes up most of present-day Turkey, supply the evidence: central Anatolia, whose early farmers show continuity with local hunter-gatherers, and northwestern Anatolia, whose Neolithic farmers are the reference for the first farmers of Europe.
The earliest farmers in the 2019 study are the aceramic farmers of Boncuklu, meaning farmers without pottery, who lived about 8300–7800 BCE; ceramic-period farmers followed them.
In central Anatolia the early farmers' ancestry is largely local: the study of the region puts their continuity with a 15,000-year-old hunter-gatherer from Pınarbaşı at about 80–90 percent.

In the models, aceramic farmers at Boncuklu derive 89.7 percent (plus or minus 3.9) of their ancestry from a population related to that hunter-gatherer, and the rest from Iranian- and Caucasus-related sources.
Later ceramic-period farmers still derive 78.7 percent (plus or minus 3.5) of theirs from those earlier farmers, adding Levant Neolithic-related ancestry.

A separate model places the split of the Anatolian and European farmer lineage from European hunter-gatherers at about 33,000–39,000 years ago, and from the Zagros farmers' lineage at about 46,000–77,000 years ago.

levant-chalcolithic-peqiin.description: Late Chalcolithic (Copper Age) individuals from Peqi'in Cave in Israel, modelled as a blend of Levantine, Iranian-related and Anatolian-related ancestry. Their mixed ancestry shows that mixing between the Near East's regional populations was already under way before the Bronze Age.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The grouping rests on one cave: all the individuals come from Peqi'in Cave and date to 4500–3900 BCE. A 2018 study analysed 22 individuals from the cave, of whom 20 appear unrelated, which matters because close relatives share much of their DNA and would count the same ancestry twice.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The study models the Peqi'in individuals as more than half (about 57 percent) Levant Neolithic-related, with the remainder related to Iran Chalcolithic (17 percent) and Anatolia Neolithic (26 percent) populations. Mixing of this kind was widespread: by the Bronze Age, Levant-, Zagros- and Anatolia-related farmer ancestries had mixed across the Near East, which reduced genetic differences between regions.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The paternal lineages of the Peqi'in males set them apart from the periods on either side. The Y chromosome passes from father to son, so its lineage, called a haplogroup, follows the paternal line: nine of the ten Peqi'in males carry the same one, haplogroup T, whereas earlier Levantine populations were dominated by haplogroup E and later Bronze Age individuals all carry haplogroup J. Because the Y chromosome follows a single line of descent, it records only part of a population's ancestry.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The three sources are not pinned down: several three-way models with similar sources fit the data, and Anatolia Neolithic and early European farmers are hard to distinguish, so each source is best read as a related population, not a named ancestor. The Peqi'in population also cannot be the sole ancestor of all later Bronze Age groups, because one Bronze Age group could not plausibly have descended from the same population.

caveats: All 20 individuals on the map come from one cave, so the footprint marks that site and not the wider southern Levant.
